mitigation_mechanism: More forest cover in a catchment lowers peak flow; the reduction is about half the change in forest cover.
caveats: Afforestation reduces peaks only gradually as the forest matures; the review also notes possible lower water availability in dry periods.
justification: Herath et al. (2025) J. Flood Risk Manag., systematic review of 50 catchment studies [source_id herath_2025_forest_cover_flood_sr], PDF p.1: "Forest cover consistently impacts peak flow across catchments of all sizes, with a generalized linear rela- tionship where the effect magnitude is approximately half the forest cover change. For example, a 20% increase in forest cover tends to reduce peak flow by 10% across small, medium, and large catchments."

mitigation_mechanism: Forest soils reduce runoff from small rainfall events but saturate in the large events that cause major downstream floods.
caveats: Local small-event benefit is acknowledged; the class reflects the stated limited influence on major floods.
justification: FAO & CIFOR (2005) Forests and floods, RAP 2005/03 [source_id fao_cifor_2005_forests_floods], PDF p.13: "Contrary to popular belief, forests have only a limited inﬂ uence on major downstream ﬂ ooding, especially large-scale events."

mitigation_mechanism: Treated catchments kept more dry-season flow, which the authors say reduced drought effects.
caveats: Bundled: exclosures (assisted regeneration) together with soil and stone bunds; Ethiopia only; no size given for the drought effect itself, so slight by rule.
justification: Meaza et al. (2022) Land Degrad. Dev., meta-analysis of 361 paired catchments (Ethiopia) [source_id meaza_2022_catchment_restoration_drought_meta], PDF p.1: "Such consistent water flow reduced hydrological, agricultural and socioeconomic drought effects in treated catchment."

mitigation_mechanism: Planted trees use more water, cutting annual runoff and, proportionally even more, low flow.
caveats: Downstream water supply in dry periods; afforestation of grasslands and shrublands, mostly plantations (eucalypts, pines). Not about on-farm soil moisture.
justification: Farley et al. (2005) Glob. Change Biol., global synthesis of 26 catchment data sets [source_id farley_2005_afforestation_water_yield], PDF p.1: "These results clearly demonstrate that reductions in runoff can be expected following afforestation of grasslands and shrublands and may be most severe in drier regions. Our results suggest that, in a region where natural runoff is less than 10% of MAP, afforestation should result in a complete loss of runoff; where natural runoff is 30% of precipitation, it will likely be cut by half or more when trees are planted. The possibility that afforestation could cause or intensify water shortages in many locations is a tradeoff that should be explicitly addressed in carbon sequestration programs."

mitigation_mechanism: Forest gain lowers land surface temperature through evapotranspiration and albedo change.
caveats: Land surface temperature, not air temperature or worker heat exposure; average forestation cooling -0.18 to -0.19 C, larger (-1.11 C) only for ~50% cover gains in the tropics.
justification: Prevedello et al. (2019) PLOS ONE, global remote-sensing analysis [source_id prevedello_2019_forestation_local_temperature], PDF p.1: "Deforestation from 2000 to 2010 caused consistent warming of 0.38 ± 0.02 (mean ± SE) and 0.16 ± 0.01˚C in tropical and temperate regions respectively, while forestation caused cooling in those regions of -0.18 ± 0.02 and -0.19 ± 0.02˚C. Tropical forests were particularly sensitive to the climate effects of forest change, with forest cover losses of ~50% associated with increased LST of 1.08 ± 0.25˚C, whereas similar forest cover gains decreased LST by -1.11"
